title: Level 1 – Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Mother and Newborn Care
intro: Welcome to GNPS Program 6 - Supporting Mothers and Newborns. Maternal and newborn nursing follows a family through pregnancy, labour, birth, postnatal recovery and the newborn's first days of life. Nurses provide observation, education, comfort and early intervention while supporting dignity, choice and family participation. This level is designed around the maternity and newborn capabilities expected within national nursing education programs and by nursing regulatory bodies across different countries. It develops the essential knowledge, assessment skills and professional behaviours required to support healthy pregnancy, safe birth, maternal recovery and newborn adaptation. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Describe normal physiological changes during pregnancy Complete routine antenatal maternal and fetal assessments Recognise pregnancy danger signs requiring urgent review Support a woman through the stages of labour Provide immediate and ongoing postnatal nursing care Perform a systematic newborn assessment Promote thermoregulation, feeding and bonding Recognise common maternal and neonatal complications Educate mothers and families about safety and self-care The condition of the mother and newborn can change quickly. A severe headache in pregnancy, abnormal fetal heart pattern, heavy bleeding after birth or newborn grunting may signal a life-threatening complication. Safe maternity care depends on knowing what is expected and acting early when findings are abnormal. By the end of Level 1, you should be able to provide safe, compassionate nursing care during pregnancy, labour, birth, postnatal recovery and early newborn life within your scope of practice. Level 1 - Qualified Nurse

content.text: Pregnancy produces major physiological and emotional changes. Most are normal adaptations, but some findings indicate risk. Antenatal nursing care supports maternal wellbeing, monitors fetal growth, promotes healthy choices and identifies problems early.
Learning outcomes
Describe common physiological changes of pregnancy Complete basic antenatal assessment
Recognise common discomforts and pregnancy danger signs Provide health education for a healthy pregnancy

Physiological Adaptations Pregnancy affects the cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal and endocrine systems. Increased blood volume, mild breathlessness, urinary frequency and fatigue may be expected, but sudden or severe symptoms require assessment.

Antenatal Assessment Assessment includes history, blood pressure, weight, urine testing, fetal growth, fetal heart activity and the mother's report of fetal movement. Screening and follow-up help identify anaemia, diabetes, infection, hypertension and fetal growth concerns.

Nutrition and Health Promotion Education should include balanced nutrition, folate and iron as recommended, physical activity, rest, immunisation guidance, avoidance of harmful substances and attendance at scheduled care.
Danger Signs Vaginal bleeding, severe headache, visual disturbance, sudden swelling, severe abdominal pain, fever, reduced fetal movement or leaking fluid require prompt evaluation.

At 32 weeks, Mrs Rao reports a severe headache, blurred vision and swelling of her hands. The nurse checks her blood pressure, performs urine testing, assesses fetal wellbeing and arranges urgent medical review. The symptoms are not dismissed as normal pregnancy discomforts.
Key learning points
Know the difference between expected changes and danger signs Monitor both maternal and fetal wellbeing
Promote early and regular antenatal care Escalate severe headache, bleeding or reduced fetal movement promptly

sections.title: Nursing Care During Labour and Birth

content.text: Labour is a dynamic process requiring ongoing assessment of the woman, fetus, contractions, pain, progress and emotional wellbeing. The nurse provides comfort, information, advocacy and timely escalation when labour deviates from the expected pattern.
Learning outcomes
Describe the stages and key features of labour Assess maternal and fetal wellbeing during labour
Provide supportive and pain-relief measures Recognise findings that require urgent intervention

Stages of Labour The first stage includes cervical dilation, the second ends with birth, the third includes placental delivery and the fourth focuses on immediate recovery. Nursing priorities change as labour progresses.

The Five Ps Labour progress is influenced by the passenger, passageway, powers, position and psyche. Assessment considers fetal position and size, pelvic factors, contractions, maternal position and emotional response.

Fetal and Contraction Monitoring The fetal heart rate, contraction frequency and duration, maternal observations and labour progress should be assessed according to the woman's risk and local policy. Abnormal patterns require prompt action.

Comfort and Support Position changes, breathing, relaxation, massage, hydration, reassurance and pharmacological pain relief can support coping. Respectful communication and informed choice remain essential.

During labour, fetal heart rate decelerations repeatedly occur after contractions. The nurse repositions the woman, stops oxytocin if running according to policy, increases assessment, calls for urgent review and prepares for further intervention. The pattern is recognised as abnormal rather than observed passively.
Key learning points
Assess the mother and fetus together Support movement, comfort and informed choice
Recognise abnormal fetal heart patterns Escalate promptly when labour or fetal wellbeing is concerning

The postnatal period involves rapid physical and emotional adjustment. Nurses monitor recovery, support feeding, promote bonding and identify complications such as haemorrhage, infection, thromboembolism and mental-health concerns.
Learning outcomes
Perform a systematic postnatal maternal assessment Recognise common postnatal complications
Support breastfeeding and maternal comfort Promote emotional wellbeing and safe discharge
Postnatal Assessment Assessment includes vital signs, uterine tone and position, lochia, bladder function, perineum or incision, pain, breasts, mobility and emotional state.

Postpartum Haemorrhage Heavy bleeding, a boggy uterus, falling blood pressure, rising pulse or increasing weakness may indicate haemorrhage. Immediate assessment, uterine massage where appropriate, emergency escalation and prescribed treatment are priorities.
Infection and Thromboembolism Fever, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling lochia, wound redness, calf pain or sudden breathlessness require urgent review.

Emotional Adaptation Mild emotional change may occur, but persistent low mood, severe anxiety, inability to function or thoughts of harm require timely mental-health assessment. Families should know how to seek help.

Two hours after birth, a woman reports dizziness and the pad is rapidly saturating with blood. The nurse assesses uterine tone and vital signs, calls for assistance, initiates the postpartum haemorrhage response and remains with the woman while treatment begins.
Key learning points
Assess bleeding and uterine tone regularly Treat heavy bleeding as an emergency
Monitor physical and emotional recovery Include support people in education with the mother's consent

The newborn must adapt rapidly to breathing, temperature control, feeding and circulation outside the uterus. Nurses support this transition, perform systematic assessment and teach families how to care safely for their baby.
Learning outcomes
Perform an immediate and ongoing newborn assessment Support thermoregulation, feeding and bonding
Recognise normal transitional findings Identify signs requiring urgent neonatal review

Immediate Adaptation Initial care focuses on airway, breathing, circulation, warmth and observation. Apgar scoring provides a structured description of adaptation but does not replace ongoing assessment.
Thermoregulation Newborns lose heat quickly. Drying, skin-to-skin contact, warm clothing and a suitable environment reduce cold stress and hypoglycaemia risk.
Feeding and Routine Care Nurses assess feeding readiness, attachment, swallowing and output. Cord care, identification, recommended prophylaxis and immunisation follow local policy.
Warning Signs Central cyanosis, grunting, retractions, persistent low temperature, poor feeding, lethargy, seizures, jaundice in the first day or signs of infection require urgent review.

A newborn appears sleepy, feeds poorly and has a low temperature. The nurse warms the baby, checks blood glucose according to policy, assesses breathing and colour, and escalates for neonatal review. These findings are not assumed to be normal sleepiness.
Key learning points
Maintain warmth from the moment of birth Assess breathing, colour, tone and feeding
Differentiate normal transition from danger signs Teach families when to seek urgent help

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 6 - Level 1, you have developed the foundational knowledge and practical skills required to support pregnancy, labour, birth, postnatal recovery and early newborn adaptation. These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse, where the focus expands to high-risk pregnancy, obstetric emergencies and complex neonatal care.
